stimulus.text:
Henry Ford, with Samuel Crowther, My Life and Work (1922), Chapter X, “How Cheaply Can Things Be Made?” (verbatim excerpt):

"The payment of high wages fortunately contributes to the low costs because the men become steadily more efficient on account of being relieved of outside worries. The payment of five dollars a day for an eight-hour day was one of the finest cost-cutting moves we ever made, and the six-dollar day wage is cheaper than the five."
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim excerpt from Henry Ford, My Life and Work (Garden City, New York: Doubleday, Page, 1922), Project Gutenberg eBook #7213, public domain.

source: original; stimulus quoted verbatim from Henry Ford, My Life and Work (1922), Project Gutenberg eBook #7213
stem: Ford's five-dollar day, announced in January 1914, is best understood as

options.text: a gift with no benefit to the company
options.misconception: Ford calls the five-dollar day a cost-cutting move. It benefited the company by cutting turnover and raising efficiency.

options.text: a law that Congress passed in 1914
options.misconception: No law set Ford's wage. Ford announced the five-dollar day in January 1914 as a company policy.

options.text: a union demand that Ford finally accepted
options.misconception: Unions did not demand the five-dollar day. Ford set it himself, and unions stayed weak in the 1920s.

options.text: a business plan to cut costs and turnover

rationales.A: Ford calls the five-dollar day a cost-cutting move. It benefited the company by cutting turnover and raising efficiency.
rationales.B: No law set Ford's wage. Ford announced the five-dollar day in January 1914 as a company policy.
rationales.C: Unions did not demand the five-dollar day. Ford set it himself, and unions stayed weak in the 1920s.
rationales.D: Background: in 1913 Ford had to hire about 50,000 men to keep an annual workforce of 15,000, so turnover was the problem the raise solved. The five-dollar day was a business plan.
rationales.general:
1. Read Ford's own words: the five-dollar day was a cost-cutting move.
2. Ask what it cut: men quit the dull line work, so hiring never stopped.
3. Add the numbers: hiring about 50,000 men to keep 15,000 jobs filled was the costly problem.
4. Name it plainly: a business plan to keep workers and raise output, not a gift.
Remember: when a boss raises pay, ask what problem the raise was meant to solve.
